title: CLI fails to match files on Windows-style backslash paths
description:
On Windows, running the CLI with a backslash-style path (e.g. .\tests\fixtures\mastermind-ls\parts\footer.html) fails with "No matching .html or .php files found for: ..." even though the file exists.

Root cause: src/cli.js:66 passes raw argv patterns directly into fast-glob (fg). fast-glob treats backslash as a glob escape character, not a path separator, so a pattern like .\tests\fixtures\mastermind-ls\parts\footer.html gets mangled into .\tests\fixturesmastermind-lsparts\footer.html (backslash + following char is consumed as an escape sequence) and never matches.

Repro (confirmed):
- fg([".\\tests\\fixtures\\mastermind-ls\\parts\\footer.html"]) -> []
- fg(["./tests/fixtures/mastermind-ls/parts/footer.html"]) -> matches correctly

Reported via: `npm start .\tests\fixtures\mastermind-ls\parts\footer.html` and `npx . .\tests\fixtures\mastermind-ls\parts\footer.html` both failing.

Suggested fix: normalize backslashes to forward slashes on each pattern before passing to fast-glob in src/cli.js, so Windows-style paths are supported.

title: bun build --compile produces a binary that cannot boot (css-tree createRequire)
description:
`npm run compile` (`bun build --compile`) produces a ~95 MiB executable that cannot start.
Parked: the blocker is in a transitive dependency, not in this repo, and there is nothing
to do here until it changes upstream.

## Symptom

Every invocation fails identically, including `--help`, which does no validation work:

```
error: Cannot find module '../data/patch.json' from 'B:\~BUN\root\wp-block-guard.exe'

Bun v1.4.0 (Windows x64)
```

The failure is at import time, before `argv` is parsed, because
`src/block-runner-adapter.js` imports `block-runner` (and therefore jsdom) at module top
level.

## Cause

```js
// node_modules/css-tree/lib/data-patch.js
import { createRequire } from 'module';
const require = createRequire(import.meta.url);
const patch = require('../data/patch.json');
```

Bun's `--compile` bundler statically analyzes literal `require`/`import` calls to decide
what to embed in the binary's virtual filesystem. A `require` constructed at runtime by
`createRequire()` is invisible to that analysis, so `patch.json` is never embedded, and the
runtime fallback resolves against `$bunfs` (`B:\~BUN\root\...`) rather than a real disk
path.

Under plain Node this works, because a relative CJS require from inside a package bypasses
that package's own `exports` restriction. The failure is specific to `--compile`.

`css-tree@3.2.1` is reached via `block-runner → jsdom → @asamuzakjp/dom-selector →
css-tree`. Three jsdom-side packages dedupe to the same copy (`npm ls css-tree`).

## What works

- `node bin/wp-block-guard.js` — the supported path, unaffected.
- `bun run bin/wp-block-guard.js` (uncompiled) — works correctly, which is what confirmed
  the in-process adapter is sound under Bun's runtime.

Only `--compile` is broken.

## Why this is parked rather than closed

A standalone executable is still a legitimate distribution goal, and the `compile` script
will begin working unchanged the day the upstream pattern changes. Nothing in this repo
needs to be undone or redesigned.

## If picked up

Two routes, neither attempted:

1. A Bun bundler plugin that handles this `createRequire`-indirected JSON require.
2. Patch or pin `css-tree` / `@asamuzakjp/dom-selector` to avoid the pattern.

Before either, re-test on a current Bun: this was measured on Bun 1.4.0, and static
analysis of `createRequire` is exactly the kind of thing Bun improves release to release.
Also re-check whether `css-tree` still ships the pattern.

Full detail: `handoff/2026-09-03-bun-compile-implementation-report.md` §5.

title: Add source field to finding schema for agent find-and-replace
description:
Add a `source` field to the finding schema so the agent-facing (JSON) output shows the
exact flagged text alongside the existing `fix` advice.

## Field order

In `makeFinding()` (`src/findings.js`), the returned object gains `source` positioned
after `message`, before `fix`:

```js
{ code, severity, file, line, blockName, message, source, fix }
```

`fix` is unchanged — it stays advisory prose for the human operator, it is not
rewritten into literal replacement code.

## What `source` contains, per finding code

| Code | `source` |
|---|---|
| `PHP_HEADER_STRIPPED` | the stripped `<?php ... ?>` header text |
| `PHP_INTERPOLATION_UNCHECKED` | the exact matched `<?...?>` fragment (captured before `maskEmbeddedPhp` blanks it) |
| `STRUCTURAL_UNBALANCED_DELIMITER`, `STRUCTURAL_MISMATCHED_CLOSER`, `STRUCTURAL_INVALID_ATTRS_JSON` | the exact delimiter comment text (`<!-- wp:name {...} -->`), sliced from the token's byte offsets already computed in `tokenizeDelimiters()` (`src/structural.js`) |
| `BLOCK_INVALID`, `BLOCK_RUNNER_WARNING` | the single source line at `item.source.htmlLine`, sliced from `body` in `src/pipeline.js` |
| `BLOCK_RUNNER_SKIPPED`, `BLOCK_RUNNER_FAILURE`, `STRUCTURAL_NO_BLOCKS` | `null` — no single location to point at |

## Touch points

- `src/findings.js` — schema field order, JSDoc for `makeFinding()`'s overrides
- `src/structural.js` — `checkStructuralBalance()` must pass through `start`/`end` (or
  the sliced text) from each token so `pipeline.js` can build `source`
- `src/php-fragment.js` — `scanForEmbeddedPhp()` must return the matched fragment text,
  not just `token` (the opener)
- `src/pipeline.js` — thread `source` into every `makeFinding()` call; for
  `BLOCK_INVALID`/`BLOCK_RUNNER_WARNING`, slice the line from `body` using
  `item.source.htmlLine`

## Also required

- `--json` output (`src/cli.js:129`) picks this up automatically once `makeFinding()`
  returns it — no separate change needed there.
- The human-formatter change to also display `source` is tracked separately (see linked
  bead) since it needs a rendering proposal first.

## Acceptance criteria

- Every finding code above produces the specified `source` value (or `null`) in both
  `br` output and `--json` output.
- `source` text is byte-exact from the input file at that point in the pipeline (no
  re-indenting/trimming beyond what's already inherent to line-slicing).
- Existing tests continue to pass; add/update fixtures covering `source` for at least
  one code from each row of the table above.

title: Set the suite's boot timeout budgets from a measured distribution (120s vs 45s is unresolved)
description:
The per-test timeout budgets introduced by wpbg-f06 rest on an unresolved inconsistency, and
there is now direct evidence that one of them is too low.

## The inconsistency

`tests/pipeline.test.js` gives the in-process warm-up hook **120s**, raised from 45s after a
verification campaign in which the hook blew 45s. `tests/cli.test.js` gives three CLI-spawning
cases **45s** for the same block-runner boot paid inside a child process, where no warm-up hook
can reach it.

Both numbers cannot be right. If a >45s boot is credible enough to require 120s in-process, the
45s child budgets are not justified by the same data. The wpbg-f06 spec review raised this and
it was deliberately deferred rather than guessed at.

## Evidence accumulated since

Three stalls have now been observed, all on this machine:

1. wpbg-f06 verification campaign 2 — the in-process warm-up hook exceeded **45s**, which is
   what produced the 120s.
2. wpbg-f06 post-review round, run 1 of 3 — `CLI wiring > exits 0 and emits a clean JSON report
   for a valid file` exceeded its **45s** budget on a run with 2.1x normal wall clock. Not
   caused by the rescoping in that round: the case carried the same 45s budget before and after.
3. Post-merge confirming runs on `develop` from the main checkout — 1 red in 5 runs. The red run
   showed `import 17.98s` against 2.44-2.63s on all four green runs, a ~7x stretch.

**45s has now been observed insufficient for a child boot on this machine.**

## The stall is I/O, not CPU

During occurrence 2 the eight cases that start a node process without booting block-runner
stayed at 1.10-2.32s, entirely normal. The stall hit the block-runner boot specifically, not
process creation generally — consistent with an I/O stall loading the 350-package
`@wordpress/*` + jsdom tree. The `import 17.98s` figure in occurrence 3 points the same way.
This machine runs OneDrive sync and a PC-manager service over the workspace.

Two consequences for the experiment design:

- Instrument **boot duration specifically**, not whole-test duration.
- A CPU-contention reproduction would likely miss the condition entirely. Earlier work on
  wpbg-f06 assumed CPU contention; that assumption now looks wrong.

## What to do

Log `Date.now()` deltas around the warm-up hook body and around the first block-runner-backed
CLI invocation, over at least ten runs, to get a real boot distribution rather than a worst
observed case. Set both constants from that distribution, and state in each comment what the
number accommodates.

Note the honest framing established on wpbg-f06: a timeout here cannot make a known start-up
cost faster. Its only useful job is catching a genuine hang. That argues for generous budgets
set from a measured distribution, not tight ones.

## Acceptance criteria

- Boot duration is measured directly and a distribution reported over >= 10 runs.
- Both constants are set from that distribution, each with a comment stating the measured cost
  it accommodates and the headroom factor.
- The full suite passes on ten consecutive runs from the **main checkout**, not only a worktree.
- If the I/O-stall hypothesis is confirmed, it is recorded where a future reader will find it.

## Out of scope

- Removing the ~10s block-runner start-up cost itself (needs the long-lived worker; separate).
- Reworking the in-process adapter or ADR 0004.

title: Spike: does a block validated in isolation match its in-document verdict?
description:
Settle one factual question: **does a block validated on its own get the same verdict as
the same block validated inside its document?**

This is the single unresolved fact standing between "per-block correction is wontfix" and
"per-block correction is cheap and worth doing". It is a spike: produce an answer, not a
feature.

## Why it matters

`wpbg-x8v` (add a `match` field carrying corrected replacement markup) is closed. Its cost
objection is now dead — with the in-process adapter, block-runner calls after the first
cost 11-36ms, so canonicalizing every invalid block in a file is fractions of a second.

What remains is correctness. Every viable design for `match` extracts one block and
canonicalizes it alone, because block-runner only ever returns whole-document output and
reformats untouched blocks in the process. That is only sound if an isolated block
validates the same way it does in context.

## What to test

Use `tests/fixtures/mastermind-ls/parts/title.html`, which has four `BLOCK_INVALID`
findings at varying nesting depths, including a paragraph two levels inside a group that is
itself invalid.

1. Validate the whole document; record each item's `block`, `status`, and `reason`.
2. Extract each block's span with `tokenizeDelimiters()` (`src/structural.js`) plus an
   opener/closer pairing pass — note `tokenizeDelimiters()` returns a flat token list and
   does no pairing; `checkStructuralBalance()` builds that stack and discards it.
3. Validate each extracted span alone. Compare verdict and reason against step 1.

Report: for how many blocks does the isolated verdict match, and where it diverges, why.

## Specific things to probe

- **Nesting depth.** Two hand-written snippets already agree with their in-document verdict
  (`hero-blob-1` valid alone and in context; `word-cloud-bg` invalid in both), but neither
  had inner blocks and neither came from the tokenizer.
- **A block whose parent is invalid.** The most likely place for divergence.
- **Blocks that inherit context** — `layout`, alignment, or theme-level attributes a parent
  supplies. If a child's `save()` output depends on ancestor attributes, isolation is
  unsound for it specifically, which may mean `match` is viable only for blocks that do not
  inherit.
- **Whether extraction must include the parent's delimiters** to preserve context, and if
  so, whether that reintroduces the overlapping-span problem that makes sequential
  find-and-replace unsafe.

## Acceptance criteria

- A written answer — yes, no, or "yes except for cases X" — with the comparison table it
  came from, recorded in `handoff/` or `archive/`.
- If isolation is sound, reopen `wpbg-x8v` and note the cost figures.
- If it is unsound, add the finding to `docs/adr/0003-no-corrected-markup-in-findings.md`
  so the ADR's "settle that before reopening" line points at a real answer.
- Either way, `wpbg-x8v`'s dependency on this bead is resolved.
close_reason: Answered: isolation matches the in-document verdict unconditionally. save() receives no block context, so validation inputs are intrinsic to the block. Write-up in handoff/2026-09-05-block-isolation-verdict-spike.md

comments.author: assistant
comments.text:
## Answered: **yes, unconditionally** — isolation matches the in-document verdict

Full write-up, both comparison tables, cost figures and caveats:
`handoff/2026-09-05-block-isolation-verdict-spike.md`.

### The short version

A block sliced at its exact delimiter span and validated alone gets the same verdict *and*
the same reason as it does inside its document. Verified on all 8 blocks of
`tests/fixtures/mastermind-ls/parts/title.html` and all 10 of a purpose-built
context-inheritance probe — **0 missing, 0 extra** in both reconciliations.

### Why it holds (this is the load-bearing part)

Not a fixture coincidence. `validateBlock`
(`@wordpress/blocks/build/api/validation/index.cjs:370`) compares exactly two things:

```js
generatedBlockContent = getSaveContent(blockType, block.attributes);
const isValid = isEquivalentHTML(block.originalContent, generatedBlockContent, logger);
```

`getSaveContent` is called with **two** arguments, so `innerBlocks` defaults to `[]` in
`getSaveElement(blockTypeOrName, attributes, innerBlocks = [])`, which calls
`save({ attributes, innerBlocks })`.

**`save()` receives no context parameter.** `usesContext`/`providesContext` is an editor and
server-render mechanism and never reaches `save()`. Ancestor `layout`, `align` or
theme-level attributes therefore cannot influence a descendant's saved markup — which was
this bead's primary suspected source of divergence.

Both validation inputs are intrinsic to the block and survive slicing byte-for-byte.

### The three probes the bead asked for

- **Nesting depth** — depths 0/1/2 all agree, from tokenizer-derived spans rather than
  hand-written snippets.
- **A block whose parent is invalid** — the paragraph at line 8 inside the invalid
  `word-cloud-bg` group: same verdict, same reason.
- **Blocks that inherit context** — `core/columns`/`core/column` (width to `flex-basis`),
  `core/buttons`/`core/button`, `core/list`/`core/list-item`. A deliberately corrupted
  `core/column` is invalid both in document and alone, identically.

### Must extraction include the parent's delimiters?

**No** — so the overlapping-span problem that would make sequential find-and-replace unsafe
does not arise.

### Cost

8 isolated validations = 128ms total (median 9ms); 10 = 29ms total (median 2ms), after the
one-time ~7.9s jsdom/Gutenberg boot already paid by the first call.

### Bearing on other beads

- **wpbg-x8v** — reopen condition met; reopening per this bead's acceptance criteria. Two
  *new* obstacles found that were not known when it was closed: canonicalize decodes HTML
  entities (not byte-preserving), and not every invalid block is repairable.
- **wpbg-djb** — unblocked. The correct item-to-block mapping can now be recovered without
  parsing `reason` prose and without patching block-runner: validate each candidate span to
  learn which blocks are genuinely invalid, then map to `items` in document order.
- **docs/adr/0003** — its "settle that before reopening" line now has a real answer.

title: Add --suggest: return the fix instead of writing it
description:
Add a `--suggest` flag that computes the fix and returns it instead of writing it, so an
agent applies the edit itself.

## Why

`--fix` is the wrong shape for an agent. `canonicalize()` does not repair the broken
blocks — it reserializes the whole document. Measured on
`tests/fixtures/mastermind-ls/parts/title.html`: 26 lines in, 28 out, and **only 2 lines
identical after trimming**. So `--fix` buries 4 real corrections in ~24 lines of churn
(re-indentation, alphabetized delimiter JSON keys, a dropped `"layout":{"type":"default"}`).

An agent that runs `--fix` has laundered a whole-file rewrite into its own change set with
no way to explain it in review. The tool should hand back what it would do and let the
agent own the edit.

This is the ecosystem norm: writing is always its own flag (`gofmt -w`, `prettier --write`,
`ruff --fix`), and the machine-readable format carries the fix rather than a mutated file.
ESLint is the closest precedent — `--fix --format json` *does* write; `--fix-dry-run` is
the opt-out.

## Scope

`--suggest` is a **standalone verb**, not a modifier of `--fix`. `--fix --suggest` together
is a usage error (exit 2): they state opposite intents about disk. This follows
`--fix-dry-run`, which likewise replaces `--fix` rather than qualifying it.

`--suggest` computes exactly what `--fix` would compute and writes nothing. The per-file
result gains one field carrying the full replacement file content:

```
"suggestedOutput": "<?php ... ?>\n<!-- wp:heading ... -->\n..."   // or null
```

It must be the **whole file**, header included — `header + fixedBody`, matching what
`--fix` writes today — so an agent can write it back without reassembling anything.

`fixMarkup()` already returns this string; `src/pipeline.js` currently assigns it to `body`
and writes it to disk without ever surfacing it on the returned result. That is the gap.

## Gating

Reuse `--fix`'s existing safety gating unchanged — embedded PHP interpolation, blocking
structural errors, nothing to fix — and report the same `fixSkippedReason`. A skipped
suggestion sets `suggestedOutput: null`. Do **not** relax the gating for `--suggest` on the
grounds that it is non-mutating: the reasons it skips are about the output being untrustworthy,
not about the write.

## Touch points

- `src/cli.js` — parse `--suggest`; reject `--fix --suggest` with exit 2.
- `src/pipeline.js` — thread a `suggest` option alongside `fix`; on that path compute
  `fixMarkup()`, skip the `fs.writeFile`, and return the result on `suggestedOutput`.
  Note the post-fix re-validate currently runs against the rewritten file — decide
  deliberately whether `--suggest` re-validates the *candidate* output (it should, so the
  reported findings describe what the agent would get).
- `src/help.js` — document the flag, the new field, and update the AGENT WORKFLOW recipe,
  which currently tells an agent to run `--fix`.
- `src/findings.js` — `BLOCK_INVALID`'s `fix` prose says "Run this tool with --fix to
  canonicalize near-miss markup". That advice is wrong for an agent on the non-mutating
  path.
- `README.md`, `tests/README.md`.

## Acceptance criteria

- `--suggest` never writes to disk. Assert the file's bytes are unchanged, not just that
  the exit code is 0.
- `suggestedOutput` is the complete file content including any stripped PHP header.
- `--fix --suggest` exits 2 with a usage error.
- `--suggest` on a clean file yields `suggestedOutput: null`, not a copy of the input.
- Gating parity with `--fix`: same skip reasons, same `fixSkippedReason` text.
- `--fix`'s existing behaviour is untouched.

## Note on line endings

The whole-document path preserved CRLF and the trailing newline on `title.html`. Do not
assume that generalises — `wpbg-8j7` tracks `--fix` stripping the trailing newline on a
different fixture, and the per-block path (see the linked bead) mangles line endings
outright. Assert the input's line-ending convention survives.
close_reason: Shipped on develop (4b1899f, ce71fba, 4d69624, 64d3fc7). --suggest returns the canonicalized whole file on suggestedOutput and writes nothing; findings, ok and the exit code keep describing the file on disk. Gating shared with --fix in both directions, suggestions re-conformed to the input's line endings and trailing newline. Suite green at 101 tests. Implementation report and findings are in the comments; the workflow split is recorded in ADR 0006.

comments.text:
> *This was generated by AI during triage.*

## Agent Brief

**Category:** enhancement
**Summary:** Add `--suggest`, a standalone verb that returns the canonicalized file content instead of writing it, so an agent applies the edit as its own change.

**Current behavior:**

The tool has one canonicalization surface, `--fix`, and it writes to disk. That serves the
**human workflow** (`wpbg <file>` to check, `wpbg <file> --fix` to fix) but is the wrong
shape for the **agent workflow**: canonicalization is whole-document, so an agent running
`--fix` launders ~24 lines of unrelated reformatting into its own change set with no way to
explain it in review.

The value the agent needs already exists and is already discarded. The adapter's
canonicalization call returns the corrected body as a string; the pipeline assigns it to
its local body variable, writes `header + body` to disk, and never surfaces it on the
returned per-file result. That omission is the whole gap.

**Desired behavior:**

`--suggest` computes exactly what `--fix` computes, writes nothing, and returns the result
as a **suggestion**: the complete file content including any stripped PHP header, so the
consumer can write it back without reassembling anything. On a file with nothing to
suggest, the value is `null` rather than a copy of the input.

`--suggest` is a standalone verb, not a modifier. `--fix --suggest` together is a usage
error (exit 2): they state opposite intents about disk. This follows `--fix-dry-run`, which
likewise replaces `--fix` rather than qualifying it.

`--suggest` belongs to the agent workflow, so it also requires `--json`, and is a usage
error (exit 2) without it. Decided during triage: the human report is built for a person
reading findings and has nowhere sensible to render a whole file, and silently ignoring the
flag would make `--suggest` a no-op that looks like it worked.

**Findings continue to describe the file on disk.** This is the one point where the bead
body above is wrong and should not be followed. It proposes that `--suggest` re-validate
and report the *candidate's* findings, mirroring what the `--fix` path does when it
discards stale findings after rewriting. That is sound for `--fix`, because the file on
disk **is** the candidate. Under `--suggest` the file on disk is untouched, so reporting
the candidate's findings would return `ok: true` and exit 0 for a still-broken file, and
would make the agent's confirming re-run meaningless.

It follows that **`--suggest` does not re-validate at all.** The re-validation on the
`--fix` path exists solely to refresh findings made stale by the write. No write, nothing
stale. The whole path is: `--fix`'s existing gates, then canonicalize, then return
`header + canonicalized` on the result — with findings, `ok`, and the exit code identical
to what a plain run of the same file reports.

That is a feature worth showing in the docs: an agent can make `--suggest --json` its
**first** call and get the findings and the suggestion together, rather than checking and
then asking for a suggestion in a second pass.

**Gating** is `--fix`'s existing gating, unchanged and unrelaxed — embedded PHP
interpolation, blocking structural errors, nothing to fix — reported through the same
skip-reason field. Do not loosen it on the grounds that `--suggest` is non-mutating: those
gates are about the output being untrustworthy, not about the write. Equally, do not
*tighten* it (see the parity criterion below).

**Key interfaces:**

- The per-file validation result gains one field carrying the suggestion: the whole file
  content as a string, or `null`. Name it for the glossary term (`suggestedOutput`).
  It sits on the **file result, not on a finding** — so it does not contradict the ADR
  refusing corrected markup in findings, whose subject is per-block correction.
- The validation entry point takes a `suggest` option alongside `fix`.
- CLI argument parsing: `--suggest`; reject `--fix --suggest`, and reject `--suggest`
  without `--json`. Both exit 2.
- The advisory `fix` prose on `BLOCK_INVALID` currently reads "Run this tool with --fix to
  canonicalize near-miss markup". That advice is wrong for a consumer on the non-mutating
  path and should account for both surfaces.

**Acceptance criteria:**

- [ ] `--suggest` never writes to disk. Assert the file's **bytes are unchanged**, not just
      that the exit code is 0.
- [ ] The suggestion is the complete file content, including a stripped PHP header where
      one was removed.
- [ ] A file with findings reports `ok: false` and exits 1 under `--suggest`, with the same
      findings a plain run of that file reports.
- [ ] A clean file yields a `null` suggestion, not a copy of the input.
- [ ] **Parity on an unrepairable file, in this direction:** verified during triage that
      `--fix` on the unfixable-extra-attribute fixture *writes* (`fixApplied: true`) and
      *still* reports the finding (`ok: false`, exit 1) — it does not refuse to write
      because a block was unrepairable. `--suggest` must match: it returns a suggestion and
      still reports the finding. It must **not** withhold the suggestion on the grounds
      that applying it would not clear the finding. Verifying that a correction actually
      resolves a finding is the blocked follow-up bead's design, not this one's.
- [ ] Gating parity with `--fix` otherwise: same skip conditions, same skip-reason text.
- [ ] `--fix --suggest` exits 2. `--suggest` without `--json` exits 2.
- [ ] The suggestion preserves the input's **trailing-newline state**, present or absent.
      Not covered by the separate trailing-newline bead: that fix belongs at the write
      call, which this path never reaches. Measured during triage on the
      unfixable-extra-attribute fixture — `--fix` returned byte-identical content minus the
      final newline (163 → 162 bytes) — so an uncorrected suggestion would have the agent
      write the same corruption back by hand.
- [ ] The suggestion preserves the input's **line-ending convention**. The whole-document
      path was observed to preserve CRLF on one fixture; do not assume that generalises —
      assert it, on both a CRLF and an LF fixture.
- [ ] `--fix`'s existing behaviour and output are unchanged.
- [ ] Help text documents the flag, the new field, and both usage errors, and the AGENT
      WORKFLOW recipe stops telling an agent to run `--fix` — it should show
      `--suggest --json` as a single first call. `README.md` and the tests README follow.

**Out of scope:**

- Per-block `match` text on individual findings — the bead blocked on this one. This bead
  emits whole-file content only, and deliberately does not verify that applying it clears
  any finding.
- Any change to `--fix`'s write behaviour, gating, or output.
- The trailing-newline bug on the `--fix` path, which stays its own bead. Only the
  suggestion's newline fidelity is in scope here.
- The stale claim in the help text's PREREQUISITES section that block-runner is invoked as
  a subprocess (superseded by the in-process ADR). Real, but a separate bead.

---

`CONTEXT.md` was updated during this triage with the terms this brief relies on —
**Human workflow**, **Agent workflow**, **Suggestion** — and `Canonicalization` was amended
to name both flags that request it.

on-disk line endings are a property of the machine and the checkout, not of the repo:

- fresh clone on Windows → **all** fixtures CRLF
- fresh clone on Linux/macOS → **all** fixtures LF

A "CRLF fixture" is therefore a local authoring artifact. An assertion resting on one
would pass here and test nothing on CI.

The line-ending tests **construct** their input byte-by-byte at runtime (joining lines
with an explicit `\r\n` or `\n` and writing the file), so they are immune to
`core.autocrlf` and to platform. `conformToSource` also has direct unit tests for the
normalization rules in isolation. Coverage of the criterion's intent is unchanged; only
the mechanism differs.

No `.gitattributes` was added. Pinning fixture endings repo-wide would renormalize files
and could invalidate line-ending measurements already recorded on other beads — worth its
own ticket if wanted, not a side effect of this one.

`wpbg-lsf` and `wpbg-hdl` both cite `title.html` as "CRLF throughout" and reason from what
canonicalization does to it. **That measurement was taken against a working-tree copy that
is committed as LF.**

The underlying finding still holds and is independently confirmed: canonicalization does
not preserve line endings. Measured during this implementation, a CRLF input came back LF
throughout with the trailing newline dropped, which is exactly why `conformToSource`
exists. But the *fixture* will not reproduce it on a fresh clone or on Linux CI, so any
test written for those beads must construct its input the same way rather than reading
`title.html` and assuming CRLF.

| `4b1899f` | Let an agent apply the fix itself with --suggest |

| `4d69624` | Record on the beads that CRLF fixtures cannot exist here |

`--suggest --json` runs `--fix`'s gates, canonicalizes, writes nothing, and returns the
whole corrected file — PHP header included — on `suggestedOutput`. `--fix` is untouched.

- `src/pipeline.js` — `validateFile(path, { fix, suggest })`. The gate block is now
  `if (fix || suggest)` with the branch in the innermost `else`, so both flags share one
  set of gates. The null-check on the canonicalization result was inverted so the existing
  `--fix` body kept its exact indentation and the diff stays readable.
- `src/cli.js` — parses `--suggest`; rejects `--fix --suggest` and `--suggest` without
  `--json`, both exit 2, both positioned after `--help`/`--version` so the flag stays
  discoverable from the tool itself. The error-path result literal carries
  `suggestedOutput: null` so the JSON shape is stable even when a file throws.
- `src/pipeline.js` — new exported `conformToSource(suggestion, raw)` (also re-exported
  from `src/index.js`).
- `src/findings.js` — `BLOCK_INVALID`'s advisory `fix` prose now names both surfaces
  instead of telling every reader to run `--fix`.
- `src/help.js`, `README.md`, `tests/README.md` — documented, including the rewritten
  AGENT WORKFLOW recipe.
- `docs/adr/0006-two-workflows-fix-writes-suggest-returns.md` and three `CONTEXT.md`
  glossary terms — see "Domain documentation" below.

## Where this deviated from the brief, and why

**1. No re-validation at all.** The ticket body asked that `--suggest` re-validate and
report the *candidate's* findings, "so the reported findings describe what the agent would
get." Not done, deliberately — the brief posted at triage already overrode this and the
implementation follows the brief.

Under `--fix` the post-write re-validate exists solely to refresh findings the write made
stale, which is correct there because after the write the file on disk **is** the
candidate. Under `--suggest` nothing is written, so nothing is stale. Reporting the
candidate's findings would return `ok: true` and exit 0 for a file still broken on disk,
and would make the agent's confirming re-run — the loop's only proof its edit worked —
meaningless.

**2. The gating is not tightened.** An earlier draft of the brief had `--suggest` withhold
the suggestion unless the candidate validated clean. That was dropped after measuring
`--fix` on `unfixable-extra-attribute.html`: it **writes** the file (`fixApplied: true`,

to write because one block is unrepairable. So a clean-only rule would have been stricter
than `--fix` rather than equal to it, and would have absorbed `wpbg-lsf`'s entire design —
verified per-block correction is that bead's job.

**3. `--suggest` requires `--json`.** Confirmed with the user during triage. The human
report has nowhere sensible to render a whole file, and silently dropping the suggestion
would make the flag look like it had worked.

**Both line-ending criteria genuinely failed on first run.** Not theoretical:

| Input | Suggestion, before the fix |
|---|---|
| CRLF x7, trailing newline | LF x6, **no** trailing newline |
| LF x3, trailing newline | LF x2, **no** trailing newline |

Hence `conformToSource`, which re-conforms a suggestion to the input's majority line-ending
convention and its trailing-newline state **in both directions** — appending
unconditionally would add a newline to a file that never had one, the same class of
unrequested edit. Verified across CRLF+newline, LF+newline, and CRLF-without-newline
inputs, plus direct unit tests of the normalization rules.

This is not covered by `wpbg-8j7`. That fix belongs immediately before the `fs.writeFile`
in the `--fix` branch — the exact line `--suggest` never reaches. Without the above, an
agent would write the corruption back by hand. `conformToSource` is exported and available
to `8j7` when it lands.

**Live reproduction of `wpbg-8j7`.** Measured during the parity check above: `--fix` on
`unfixable-extra-attribute.html` returned byte-identical content minus the final newline,
163 → 162 bytes. The entire md5 change was the trailing newline.

**"A CRLF fixture and an LF fixture" is unsatisfiable in this repo.** Detailed in a
separate comment on this bead and on `wpbg-lsf`. Summary: every fixture is committed as LF,
`core.autocrlf=true`, no `.gitattributes`, so on-disk endings are a property of the machine
— CRLF everywhere on a fresh Windows clone, LF everywhere on Linux. The line-ending tests
therefore **construct** their inputs byte-by-byte. No `.gitattributes` was added;
renormalizing repo-wide could invalidate measurements recorded on other beads and deserves
its own ticket.

**No fixture could prove header re-attachment.** The criterion "the complete file content,
including a stripped PHP header" had nothing to run against: `pattern-with-header.php`
validates clean and short-circuits on the `errorCount === 0` gate, while
`pattern-with-interpolation.php` and `interpolated-delimiter-attrs.php` both trip the
embedded-PHP gate first. It is also the one criterion where returning the body alone passes
every other test. Added `tests/fixtures/wp-block-guard/pattern-with-header-invalid-heading.php`

before writing the assertion.

per-file position mapping is re-derived per result, so a multi-file run is where a
suggestion could be misattributed. Verified correct across a three-file glob — one
repairable, one with two findings, one clean — and asserted by corrected-heading count per
file, which a crossed suggestion would fail. Consequence documented rather than left as a
surprise: a wide glob returns every corrected file in one payload.

- `--suggest` leaves the file byte-identical, compared as `Buffer`s rather than strings.
- `suggested.findings` deep-equals `plain.findings` for the same file, with `ok` and

`docs/adr/0006-two-workflows-fix-writes-suggest-returns.md` records why the surface divides

A skipped suggestion reports through `fixSkippedReason` — a fix-named field on the
non-`--fix` path. Kept because the criterion was *same skip-reason text*, and introducing a

title: --fix strips the file's trailing newline
description:
`--fix` rewrites files without their final newline.

## Repro

`tests/fixtures/wp-block-guard/invalid-heading-missing-class.html` ends with `\n`. After a
`--fix` run the rewritten file does not:

```
input      endsWithNewline=true   tail="2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->\n"
after fix  endsWithNewline=false  tail="h2>\n<!-- /wp:heading -->"
```

## Cause

block-runner's canonicalized markup (`report.output`) carries no trailing newline, and
`src/pipeline.js` writes `header + fixedBody` verbatim.

Pre-existing, and **not** a regression from the in-process adapter: the old subprocess
`--out` path and the new `canonicalize()` call were compared on the same input and produce
byte-identical output, trailing newline included (i.e. absent in both).

## Why it is worth fixing

Every file a user fixes gains a spurious one-line diff, and POSIX tooling flags
newline-at-EOF loss. It is noise attributable to this tool, in files the user did not
otherwise change.

## Suggested fix

In `src/pipeline.js`, preserve the input's trailing-newline state when writing the fixed
body: if `raw` ended with a newline and the fixed body does not, append one. Do not
unconditionally append — that would add a newline to files that never had one.

## Acceptance criteria

- A `--fix` run preserves the input file's trailing-newline state, present or absent.
- Regression test covers both directions.

title: vitest discovers test files written into .scratch/
description:
`vitest.config.js` excludes `.claude/worktrees/**` from test discovery but does **not** exclude
`.scratch/**`. Any file matching vitest's default test glob that is written into `.scratch/`
gets discovered and run as part of the suite.

Found by accident during wpbg-f06: an agent wrote a throwaway probe file into `.scratch/` while
measuring block-runner boot timings, and the full suite reported **159** cases instead of 157.

## Why it matters, and why it is not urgent

`.scratch/` is gitignored, so this cannot affect CI or another checkout — it only ever bites the
person whose working copy holds the scratch file. But `CLAUDE.md` describes `.scratch/` as
"temporary space for ad-hoc operations" that is "safe to write to freely", which is precisely an
invitation to put a file there that vitest will then execute. A stray probe that throws, or that
asserts something false, turns into a red suite with no obvious cause.

This is the same class of trap the `.claude/worktrees/**` exclusion already exists to prevent.

## Suggested fix

Add `.scratch/**` alongside the existing exclusion, preserving the `...configDefaults.exclude`
spread:

```js
exclude: [...configDefaults.exclude, '.claude/worktrees/**', '.scratch/**'],
```

Consider whether `.firecrawl/**` warrants the same treatment — `CLAUDE.md` describes it in the
same terms, as gitignored agent output space.

## Acceptance criteria

- A test-shaped file placed in `.scratch/` is not discovered by `npx vitest list`.
- The existing `.claude/worktrees/**` exclusion and the `configDefaults.exclude` spread both
  still work, verified from the main checkout.
- `tests/README.md`'s description of the exclude list matches the config exactly.

description:
> *This was generated by AI during triage.*

The `PREREQUISITES` section of the CLI help text still describes block-runner as being
invoked as a subprocess. ADR 0004 superseded that in 2026-09-03; Layer 2 now imports
block-runner's library API and calls it in-process.

## Current text

> block-runner is installed as this package's own dependency and is invoked directly (its
> resolved bin script via node), not through "npx", specifically to avoid npx's own
> package-resolution overhead (measured at ~12s/call versus block-runner's own ~0.1-0.2s
> of actual work).

Two things are now wrong. There is no bin script invocation — the adapter imports
`validate` and `canonicalize` directly. And the npx comparison, while still true, is no
longer the reason for anything: the operative reason is that booting jsdom and the
`@wordpress/*` tree costs ~10s and the CLI validates files in a loop, so a per-file
subprocess made a 68-file theme take roughly ten minutes.

## Why it is worth fixing

This section is addressed to a reader "deciding whether to trust this output", so it is
read by exactly the audience least able to check it against the source. It also states a
performance model that would lead someone to expect per-file process isolation the tool no
longer has — which matters, because ADR 0004 records that a block-runner crash can now take
our own process down, and that `captureStderr()` patching a global is only sound while file
processing stays sequential.

## Scope

Documentation only. No behaviour change, and no revisiting of ADR 0004's decision.

- Rewrite `PREREQUISITES` to describe in-process invocation and give the loop-boot reason
  rather than the npx one.
- Check `README.md` for the same claim.

## Acceptance criteria

- The help text no longer describes block-runner as invoked as a subprocess or via its bin
  script.
- The stated reason for the invocation strategy matches ADR 0004's (one-time boot across a
  file loop), not the npx-overhead one.
- `README.md` carries no contradicting claim.
- The Node >= 20 requirement is retained.

# wpbg-dpw: colorize the human-readable report, surface `search`

Implements the design approved 2026-09-07 (option 1: color only, existing
layout unchanged) superseding the ticket body's "Not yet decided" section.

## What changed

### `src/report.js`

- Added a hand-rolled ANSI table (`ANSI = { red, green, yellow, cyan, gray,
  reset }`) — no new dependency, per the approved design.
- `formatHuman(report, { strict, color })` now takes an explicit `color`
  boolean instead of reading `process.stdout.isTTY` / `process.env.NO_COLOR`
  itself, so it stays a pure function of its inputs. A `paint(code, text)`
  closure applies `${code}${text}${reset}` only when `color` is true;
  everywhere colorized text is built by calling `paint(...)` instead of a
  scattered `if (color)` per line.
- Colorized exactly the scope the design specifies, nothing more:
  - Status line: `statusMark`/`status` — green for PASS, red for FAIL.
  - Finding marker + `[CODE]` — red/yellow/cyan by `severity`, via a new
    `SEVERITY_COLOR` map keyed the same way as the existing `MARKERS` map.
  - The whole `fix:` line — gray.
  - Summary line: only the `N error(s)` and `N warning(s)` substrings are
    tinted, and **only when the count is nonzero** — see "Deviation" below.
- Added a `search:` line, printed after the message line and before the
  `fix:` line, matching `makeFinding()`'s key order
  (`code, severity, file, line, blockName, message, search, fix`).
  `truncateSearch()` takes the first line only, caps it at 80 chars, and
  appends `…` when the value was truncated or was multi-line to begin with.
  Omitted entirely when `finding.search == null` (never prints
  `search: null`).
- `search` is byte-exact input text, so a CRLF file's first line ends in a
  literal `\r`. Printed as-is, that trailing CR returns the terminal cursor
  to column 0 and the `…` overwrites the start of the line instead of
  appending to the end. `truncateSearch()` strips a trailing `\r` from the
  extracted first line before capping/appending the ellipsis. This wasn't in
  the original brief; caught by the advisor review, not by either code-review
  sub-agent or my first test pass — added a dedicated CRLF regression test.

### `src/cli.js`

- Added `shouldColorize({ isTTY, noColor } = {})`, mirroring the existing
  `normalizePatternsForPlatform(patterns, platform)` pattern: it defaults its
  params from `process.stdout.isTTY`/`process.env.NO_COLOR` but accepts
  injected values, so tests can assert both true/false states without faking
  a real TTY.
- `main()`'s non-JSON branch now calls
  `formatHuman(report, { strict: flags.strict, color: shouldColorize() })`.
  `--json` takes a separate branch above this and never calls `formatHuman`
  at all — per the brief, I did **not** add a redundant `if (!flags.json)`
  check inside the color computation; it's structurally unreachable already.
  Covered by an end-to-end test asserting `--json` output has no ANSI
  escapes, without adding a runtime branch that pretends otherwise.

### Tests

- New `tests/report.test.js` (14 cases): color on/off per severity and
  status, `fix:` line dimming, summary-count tinting including the
  zero-count exception, `search` line presence/omission/truncation
  (short/long/multi-line/CRLF), and search-vs-fix line ordering.
- `tests/cli.test.js`: added `shouldColorize` unit tests (TTY×NO_COLOR
  matrix) and three end-to-end CLI checks — non-TTY (piped) output has no
  ANSI, `--json` has none regardless of `NO_COLOR`, and an explicit
  `NO_COLOR=1` run has none. The `NO_COLOR=1` end-to-end case is redundant
  with `shouldColorize`'s own non-TTY suppression (spawnSync always pipes
  stdout), but it pins the acceptance criterion end-to-end rather than only
  at the unit level, per a gap the spec-review sub-agent flagged.
- Did not touch `src/findings.js`, `src/block-locator.js`, or
  `src/pipeline.js` (reserved for the concurrent `wpbg-lsf` work).

title: cli.test.js flakes under CPU contention, producing false red suites
description:
A single `tests/cli.test.js` case intermittently exceeds its 25s timeout when the suite runs
under CPU contention. It passes in isolation and on an unloaded machine, so it is a test-budget
problem rather than a product defect — but it has now produced a false "the suite is red" signal
three separate times, which is expensive because each occurrence has to be investigated before
any merge can proceed.

## Occurrences (all 2026-09-12, all on different changesets)

| Where | Symptom |
|---|---|
| `wpbg-dpw` implementation | `CLI --suggest > reports suggestedOutput as null for a clean file` timed out at 25s in a `cli.test.js`-only run; passed alone (14s) and in the full run |
| `wpbg-zxg` implementation | Full-suite failure reported, verified as the same pre-existing flake; `cli.test.js` passes 25/25 in isolation |
| `wpbg-ztf` / `wpbg-hdl` verification | 156/157 on two consecutive full runs in the `wpbg-ztf` worktree, then **157/157** on a third; the `wpbg-hdl` agent saw the identical single failure in its own unrelated docs-only worktree at the same time |

The `wpbg-ztf` and `wpbg-hdl` occurrences are the clearest evidence: both worktrees contained
**documentation-only** changes that cannot affect runtime behaviour, and both were running
concurrently, competing for CPU.

## Likely cause

`cli.test.js` spawns the CLI as a subprocess many times, and each spawn pays block-runner's
jsdom + `@wordpress/*` cold-start (~10s, per `src/help.js`'s own note and
`docs/adr/0004-in-process-block-runner-invocation.md`). ADR 0004 moved block-runner in-process
precisely so that cost is paid once per *run* — but a spawned CLI subprocess is a fresh process
and pays it again. Under load, one of those spawns crosses 25s.

## Possible directions (none investigated; this ticket is the investigation)

- Raise the timeout for the CLI-spawning tests specifically, rather than globally.
- Reduce how many tests need a real subprocess — some may be able to call `main(argv)` in-process.
- Serialize or pool the CLI-spawning tests so they don't contend with each other.
- Warm block-runner once and share it, if the spawn boundary allows.

Measure before choosing: confirm the cold start is actually where the time goes, rather than
assuming it from the ADR.

## Acceptance criteria

- The specific failing case is identified by name and its timing characterised under both idle
  and loaded conditions.
- The full suite passes reliably when another CPU-heavy process is running — the condition that
  reproduces it today.
- If the resolution is a raised timeout, it is scoped to the tests that need it and carries a
  comment explaining why, so it does not read as an arbitrary number.
- No reduction in what the tests actually assert.

> *This was generated by AI during triage.*

## Agent Brief

**Category:** bug
**Summary:** The first block-runner-touching test in each test file absorbs a ~9–10s
per-process block-runner boot; under the suite's own parallelism that boot stretches past the
25s per-test budget, producing intermittent false-red suites.

## Verification (2026-09-16)

Reproduced on the **first** full-suite run, on an otherwise **idle** machine — no external
CPU-heavy process was needed. `155/157`, two timeouts:

| Failing case | Position |
|---|---|
| `cli.test.js > CLI wiring > exits 0 and emits a clean JSON report for a valid file` | first test in the file |
| `pipeline.test.js > validateFile — clean cases > validates a clean core/heading block with no findings` | first test in the file |

The failure is not random: in each file it is the **first test that touches block-runner**.

### Timing characterisation

`pipeline.test.js` run in isolation: `60/60`, 21.8s wall.

| Case | Duration |
|---|---|
| First test in the file | **9,183ms** |
| Every other in-process case, including all `--fix` / `canonicalize` cases | **6–66ms** |
| `block-runner stderr containment > does not leak block-runner output to stderr on a --fix run` | **9,872ms** |

That last case is the only one in the file that spawns the CLI as a child process — which is
exactly why it is the only non-first case costing seconds.

`cli.test.js` invokes the CLI via `spawnSync` per case, so each case pays a fresh boot. Its
block-runner-touching cases measured 8.6s, 8.7s, 8.7s, 8.9s, 9.2s, 9.7s and 17.5s against the
25s budget — steady-state, with no headroom.

Full suite: 6 test files across 12 cores, 224s wall against 310s of summed test time, i.e.
genuinely parallel. The ~9s idle boot stretches past 25s under that parallelism — roughly a
2.7x stretch.

### One model explains all of it

**block-runner costs ~9–10s to boot, and that cost is paid once per OS process.** After the
boot, in-process work is milliseconds. Anything that crosses a process boundary pays it again.

## Two corrections to this ticket's existing record

Both were assumed rather than measured, and a fix built on either would target the wrong thing.

1. **The prior triage comment's supporting evidence is wrong.** It states that
   `pipeline.test.js` "does not spawn the CLI; it calls `validateFile` in-process". It *does*
   spawn, in the `block-runner stderr containment` case. Its conclusion — cold boot rather than
   the process boundary — still holds for the case that actually failed, but the stated
   reasoning does not survive and should not be carried forward as given.

2. **The `45000`-ms timeouts on two `validateFile — --fix` cases rest on a stale claim.** Their
   comment reads "3 block-runner spawns happen in this test (~10s each steady-state)". Measured
   today: **28ms and 46ms**. Those numbers predate ADR 0004 moving block-runner in-process.
   This also disposes of the theory that `canonicalize()` is expensive per call — it is not.

## Current behavior

A full-suite run intermittently reports one or two timeout failures in cases that pass in
isolation. Each occurrence has to be investigated before a merge can proceed; this has now
happened five times, twice on provably documentation- or comment-only changesets.

## Desired behavior

A full-suite run is deterministic with respect to block-runner start-up: repeated runs on the
same tree produce the same pass/fail result, and that result does not change when the machine
is under load or when a second suite runs concurrently. A failure in the suite means a real
defect.

## Key facts a fix must respect

- The boot cost is **per process**, not per call and not per file. A remedy scoped only to
  "the tests that spawn the CLI" leaves the first in-process case in each worker exposed, and
  vice versa.
- `cli.test.js` paying a full boot per `spawnSync` is a **structural** cost, not a budgeting
  accident. Raising a timeout does not remove it, and the margin there is already thin.
- The stderr-capture design in the block-runner adapter is only sound because files are
  processed one at a time (see ADR 0004). Do not introduce concurrency into that path as part
  of this work.
- Vitest's per-file worker isolation is what multiplies the boot by the number of
  block-runner-touching files.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The full suite passes on ten consecutive runs on an idle machine.
- [ ] The full suite passes while a second full suite runs concurrently — the condition the
      earlier occurrences were observed under.
- [ ] No test's assertions are weakened or removed, and no test is skipped.
- [ ] Any timeout value that remains raised is scoped to the cases that need it and carries a
      comment stating the measured cost it accommodates.
- [ ] The two stale `45000` timeouts on the `--fix` cases are corrected or removed, since the
      cost they cite has been measured at ~30–50ms.
- [ ] Measured before-and-after timings are reported for the first block-runner-touching case
      in each affected file.

## Out of scope

- Removing the ~10s block-runner start-up cost from the product itself. That is the separate,
  still-open performance issue recorded in `README.md`, and it needs a long-lived worker
  process. This ticket is about the test suite's exposure to that cost, not the cost.
- Changing what any test asserts, or the product code under test.
- Reworking the in-process adapter or revisiting ADR 0004.
- The parked `bun build --compile` issue, which shares block-runner as a dependency but nothing
  else.

> *This was generated by AI during triage.*

## Correction to the agent brief: the mechanism is a boot *window*, not a uniform slowdown

The brief above characterises the parallel full run as stretching the ~9s block-runner boot
"roughly 2.7x". **That is wrong**, and it points an implementer at the wrong remedy. The
correct mechanism, from the same run's data:

In the parallel full run where the two first-in-file tests blew the 25s budget, the
**non-first** boots in `cli.test.js` cost 8680, 8689, 8672, 8915, 9169, 9212 and 9680ms — one
outlier at 17466ms. Those are essentially the 9183ms measured in isolation. If parallelism
inflated every boot 2.7x they would have landed near 23s. They did not. `pipeline.test.js`'s
in-process cases ran at 12-53ms in the parallel run, identical to isolation: no degradation at
all.

So parallelism does not inflate boots generally. **Only the boots that land in the run's
opening window get starved**; everything after runs at near-idle speed. The number that shows
the window directly is import time: **48.27s summed across 6 files** in the parallel run
against **1.33s** for `pipeline.test.js` alone. Six workers loading the 350-package
`@wordpress/*` + jsdom tree simultaneously is the contention, and it is front-loaded.

## Confirmation: the suite is green when the window is removed

`--no-file-parallelism`, same tree, no other change:

| Metric | Parallel run | Serial run |
|---|---|---|
| Result | 155/157 (two timeouts) | **157/157** |
| Summed import time | 48.27s | **2.44s** |
| First test, `cli.test.js` | **timeout at 25s** | 8,136ms |
| First test, `pipeline.test.js` | **timeout at 25s** | 7,127ms |
| CLI-spawning case in `pipeline.test.js` | 9,872ms | 8,100ms |
| Wall clock | 224.33s | **119.38s** |

Per-boot cost is unchanged at ~7-8s; only the collision is gone. The serial run is also
**faster in wall-clock terms** than the parallel one, which is worth knowing before treating
file parallelism as a throughput win worth preserving here.

## What this changes for the fix

This does not prescribe a direction, but it rules one out and surfaces one:

- **Warming block-runner once in a setup hook** — the direction the earlier triage comment
  favoured — still executes inside the opening window. It changes which timer is running while
  the cost is paid, not whether the cost collides. Do not assume it works without measuring.
- **Staggering or serialising the block-runner-touching files**, or excluding boot time from
  the per-test budget, targets the window itself. `--no-file-parallelism` is a live, verified
  remedy already, though whether it is the right one (it serialises the four files that do not
  need it either) is the implementer's call.

The acceptance criteria in the brief above stand unchanged.

# wpbg-f06 — test-suite flake under block-runner boot contention

**Status:** implemented, verified. Bead left open for the maintainer to close.
**Branch:** `worktree-agent-ad6e0a81a493bcb8f`
**Machine:** 12-core Windows 11, Node ≥20, vitest 4.1.11. Every number here was
measured on this machine. The figures in triage comments #36/#37 came from a
different machine and are **not** reused as a baseline.

## The mechanism, stated precisely

block-runner loads jsdom + the `@wordpress/*` tree **lazily, at its first
`validate()` call** — not at import. Probed directly:

| Step | Cost |
|---|---|
| `import('block-runner')` | 1.1–1.3s |
| first `validate()` | 10.3s / 14.4s |
| second `validate()` | 2–3ms |

Because the boot happens at first call, it lands inside a **test body**, and so
inside that test's timeout budget. That is the whole bug, and it explains why the
casualty was always "the first block-runner-touching test in the file" and never
a later one.

Two things follow, and they need different remedies:

- The boot is paid **once per OS process**. Under `fileParallelism`, every worker
  that pays one starts inside the same opening window and they starve each other.
- Whoever runs first **absorbs** the cost. That is an attribution problem, and it
  is independent of contention.

The fix addresses both, separately.

## What changed

Four files. No product code, no assertion changed, no test skipped, no
concurrency introduced into the adapter path.

### `vitest.config.js`

- `fileParallelism: false` — removes the contention window. Also moves the suite
  strictly to the safe side of ADR 0004, whose `captureStderr()` is only sound
  while one block-runner call is in flight.
- `testTimeout` 25000 → **5000** (vitest's default), so that every remaining
  raised budget has to justify itself locally.
- `.claude/worktrees/**` exclusion preserved verbatim.

### `tests/pipeline.test.js`

- **A `beforeAll` warm-up hook** pays the one in-process boot, keeping it out of
  any individual test's budget.
- **All 21 blanket `}, 45000)` timeouts removed**, including the two stale ones
  the ticket named.
- One scoped budget kept: the `block-runner stderr containment` case, which
  spawns the CLI and so pays a boot in a child the hook cannot reach.

### `tests/cli.test.js`

- Three per-case timeouts (`30000`, `45000`, `45000`) removed.
- `ONE_BOOT_BUDGET_MS` (45s) on the three describe blocks that spawn;
  `TWO_BOOT_BUDGET_MS` (90s) on the single case that spawns twice. The two
  pure-unit blocks stay on the 5s default.
- A warm-up is not available here: the boot happens in the child process.

### `tests/README.md`

Rewritten "Running the tests" section plus a new "Timeouts and the block-runner
boot" section holding the **measurement table**, which is now the single source
for every figure cited in the three files above.

## Measured before / after

Before = 3 baseline runs on the unmodified tree (2 file-parallel, 1 serial).
After = 10 consecutive runs on the final tree. min / median / **max**, ms.

| Case | Before | After | Budget |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pipeline.test.js > validateFile — clean cases > validates a clean core/heading block…` | 7427 / 7970 / **11043** | 5 / 5 / **7** | 25s → 5s default |
| `cli.test.js > CLI wiring > exits 0 and emits a clean JSON report…` | 8291 / 9016 / **12692** | 8211 / 8306 / **10806** | 25s → 45s |
| `pipeline.test.js > block-runner stderr containment…` | 8964 / 10332 / **12515** | 8257 / 8324 / **8488** | 45s → 45s |
| `cli.test.js > CLI wiring > --strict turns a warning-only file…` | 16798 / 19223 / **23061** | 16451 / 16592 / **18117** | 30s → 90s |

The **spread** is the result to read, not the medians:

| Case | Before max−min | After max−min |
|---|---|---|
| cli first case | 4401ms | **2595ms** |
| stderr containment | 3551ms | **231ms** |
| `--strict` | 6263ms | **1666ms** |

That collapse in variance is the bug being fixed. The old failures were the top
of those ranges crossing a budget; the ranges no longer reach it.

**Read the first row carefully.** It did not get faster — the boot *moved*, out
of the test and into the warm-up hook, which vitest does not report as a test
duration. The honest framing is: that case went from ~8s to milliseconds, and the
boot it used to carry is now a hook costing about the same as before. Total work
is unchanged, which the file's wall clock confirms:
`pipeline.test.js` alone went **30.2s → 24.1s** (not slower; the saving is the
removed second boot the old first-test/`-t` path could incur).

The last row is the case triage had **not** identified. It makes two
block-runner-backed CLI invocations back to back, and at 23.1s against its old
**30000** budget it was 77% consumed — thinner than either case the ticket names.
Serialisation alone would not have made it safe: it was still 16.8s serial. This
is why the fix is serialisation **and** measured budgets, not either alone.

## Run counts

Three designs were measured, not one. All three campaigns are shown, including
the one that failed.

| # | Condition | Runs | Result | Wall clock |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| — | Baseline, unmodified tree, file-parallel | 2 | 157/157 both | 125.1s, 128.5s |
| — | Baseline, unmodified tree, `--no-file-parallelism` | 1 | 157/157 | 127.3s |
| 1 | Design A (serialise + per-case budgets), ten consecutive | 10 | 157/157 every run | 119.3–154.3s |
| 1 | Design A, concurrent pair | 2 | 157/157 both | 170.5s, 170.4s |
| — | Design A, `-t "<one pipeline case>"` | 1 | **FAILED** (5s timeout) | — |
| 2 | Design B (+ warm-up hook at 45s), ten consecutive | 10 | **9/10 green**; run 1 failed 97/157 | 121.8–225.9s |
| 3 | Design C (hook at 120s), ten consecutive | **10** | **157/157 every run** | **121.4–127.6s** |
| 3 | Design C, two full suites concurrently | **2** (1 pair) | **157/157 both** | 143.5s, 143.5s |
| 3 | `pipeline.test.js` alone | 1 | 60/60 | 24.1s |
| 3 | `-t` filter checks (2 shapes) | 2 | both pass | 9.1s, 3.7s |

Total ≈ 40 full-suite runs, ~90 minutes of test time. The AC's ten-consecutive
and concurrent-pair criteria are satisfied by campaign **3**, on the final tree.

Design C's wall clock is also the tightest of everything measured (121.4–127.6s,
a 6.2s spread across ten runs), against the baseline's 125.1/128.5/127.3s and
Design B's 121.8–225.9s.

## A regression I introduced and then fixed

Worth recording, because it is the same bug wearing different clothes.

Dropping the global timeout to 5s while leaving the boot on pipeline.test.js's
first test made the **full** suite reliable but broke **focused** runs:

```
npx vitest run tests/pipeline.test.js -t "slices a post-fix finding from the rewritten file"
→ FAILED, 5s timeout
```

A filtered run has no predecessor to have warmed anything, so the case had to pay
the boot itself. I had converted an intermittent false red in full runs into a
deterministic false red in focused runs — and focused runs are a first-class
workflow here (this bead's own history is full of them). The `beforeAll` warm-up
is what fixes it; that case now passes in 9.1s.

Verified after the fix:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `-t "<a pipeline case>"` | passes, 9.1s |
| `-t "<a cli unit case>"` (whole suite) | passes, 3.7s total |

The second confirms the warm-up hook does **not** fire for a file with no
matching tests, so focused runs elsewhere don't pay a pointless boot.

## The hook timeout I raised from 45s to 120s — read this sceptically

The sequence "campaign fails, raise a timeout, campaign passes" is structurally
the same move that produced this bead's four prior occurrences. It deserves the
scrutiny, so here is the full account rather than a summary.

Design B put the warm-up hook on a 45s budget (~3.2x the 13.9s worst boot I had
measured). On run 1 of ten, the hook timed out:

```
pipeline.test.js — Hook timed out in 45000ms.   → 97 passed, 60 failed
```

All 60 failures are that one file: a failed `beforeAll` fails every test under
it. Runs 2–10 were clean.

**What I can and cannot tell you about that run.** That run's wall clock was
225.9s against ~122s for its nine neighbours. But `cli.test.js` inside it took
103,196ms against run 2's 101,507ms — 1.7% apart. So there was *no* machine-wide
stall spanning the run; whatever happened was localized to the pipeline file.
Roughly 74s of that run's wall clock is unattributed (cli 103s + hook 45s +
others ~4s ≈ 152s against 226s observed).

The explanation that fits both facts: a timed-out hook does not cancel the boot
already in flight. Vitest abandons the promise at 45s, but jsdom and the
`@wordpress/*` tree keep loading in that worker, which cannot exit until they
finish. The unattributed 74s is then teardown waiting on abandoned work — an
*effect* of the timeout, not evidence of its cause.

**I therefore cannot recover what the boot actually cost on that run.** It may
have been ~50–60s; it is not distinguishable from a longer stall with the data I
kept. I did not re-instrument to find out, and that is a real gap.

**Why 120s is nonetheless the right number, independent of that run.** The
argument is not "it made the campaign green":

- A timeout on this hook cannot make the boot faster. The boot is a known, fixed,
  out-of-scope cost (`README` "Known issues"). The only thing a budget here can
  usefully catch is block-runner genuinely *hanging*, and 120s catches that.
- A hook failure amplifies to 60 red tests, not one. That asymmetry justifies
  being more conservative here than anywhere else in the suite.
- Every other budget in this change was left untouched at 45s/90s and was green
  across all three campaigns. The 120s re-qualifies the hook alone.

If a reviewer disagrees, the cheap experiment is to log `Date.now()` deltas
around the hook body and run ten; that yields a real boot distribution rather
than the single censored observation above.

## What I tried and rejected

**Splitting into vitest `projects` so only the two block-runner files serialise.**
Rejected on measurement, as the ticket required — not assumed. The four files
touching neither block-runner nor a subprocess hold 72 cases totalling ~15ms of
real test time; their cost is entirely worker start-up:

| | Parallel | Serial |
|---|---|---|
| The four cheap files alone | 4.29s | **2.71s** |

They are *faster* serially. There is no parallelism win to preserve, so a
projects split would add configuration (and, per vitest semantics, force
replicating the `.claude/worktrees/**` exclusion per project, which is easy to
drop) to buy a negative amount of wall clock.

**A warm-up hook *instead of* serialising.** This is what comment #37 rejected,
and #37 is right: warming still executes inside the contended opening window, so
it does not fix contention. It fixes *attribution*. The two are complementary and
the final design uses both — I've written that reasoning into the hook's comment
so the next reader doesn't think the correction was re-litigated.

**`isolate: false`** (shared module registry across files in one fork) would
genuinely remove a boot, but trades real test isolation for ~10s on a ~130s run.
Rejected.

**Raising timeouts while keeping file parallelism.** Leaves the variance in place
and merely widens the band.

## Deliberately left undone

- **The ~10s block-runner boot itself.** Out of scope; it is the open performance
  issue in `README.md` and needs a long-lived worker process.
- **`cli.test.js` paying a boot per `spawnSync`.** Structural. Removing it means
  either converting cases to in-process `main(argv)` calls — which would weaken
  what they assert, since the file exists to exercise the real binary — or the
  long-lived worker above.
- **Stale `README "Known issues" #N` cross-references** in other test comments.
  The README's numbering has changed (one open issue remains, now #1), so several
  `#2`/`#3` references no longer resolve. I removed those attached to timeouts I
  deleted; I did not sweep the rest. Unrelated to this bead.
- **`.scratch/**` is not in vitest's `exclude`.** Found by accident: a scratch
  probe file of mine was discovered by the full suite (159 cases instead of 157).
  Harmless today — `.scratch/` is gitignored and normally holds no test files —
  but a real trap. Flagged, not fixed; it is a separate change.
- **ADR 0004's "11–36ms" figure for post-boot in-process calls.** I measured
  2–160ms on this suite's fixtures. The ADR's *conclusion* is unaffected, and
  reworking it is explicitly out of scope, so I recorded the re-measurement in
  `tests/README.md` rather than silently contradicting the ADR or editing it.

## Honest limits of this verification

The unmodified tree **did not reproduce the failure on this machine**: it passed
3/3, and parallel vs serial wall clock differed by under 3s, against triage's
224s vs 119s. So the green campaign shows the fix does not break anything and
that the margins are now wide; it is **not** a demonstration that this machine
reproduced the bug and the fix cured it.

The evidence that the fix targets the real mechanism is the timing model (boot at
first `validate()`, once per process, inside a test's timer), the before/after
**spread** rather than the medians, and the fact that every maximum drops. A
confirming run on the maintainer's machine — which does reproduce — is still
worth having.

## Worktree exclusion

Cannot be run from the main checkout from inside an isolated worktree, so the
condition was reproduced locally: a throwaway
`.claude/worktrees/probe/tests/dummy.test.js` containing a deliberately failing
assertion was created inside this worktree and `npx vitest list` run against it.

- The dummy was **not** discovered.
- Exactly **157** cases were listed.

That exercises the same nested-path shape the main checkout sees. **The maintainer
should still confirm once from the main checkout**, since that is the tree the
exclusion actually protects.

## Review

Ran `/code-review` (Standards + Spec axes). Both reports were acted on:

- Spec axis flagged the `CLI wiring` describe carrying a 90s budget for cases
  measured at 1.1–2.5s → the 90s is now on the single two-boot case only.
- Standards axis flagged `tests/README.md` as contradicted by the diff, the
  measurement narrative being triplicated and drifting between the three sites,
  cost-named constants holding budgets, and the silent divergence from ADR 0004's
  figure → all addressed, with `tests/README.md` now the single source.

title: Spike: can match be produced for a block with children?
description:
Answer one question: can a `match` value be produced for a block that **has children**, or is leaf-only the permanent ceiling? `wpbg-lsf` emits `match: null` for any block with children, unconditionally, because a parent's correction cannot be spliced as-is. This spike decides whether that is a temporary limitation or the end of the road. **Do not implement inside this bead** — produce a verdict and a recommendation. ## Why it is not obvious Validation strips inner blocks, so `canonicalize` returns a parent with its children gone. Measured on `tests/fixtures/mastermind-ls/parts/title.html`, the L1 `core/group` has 3 children and comes back as: ```html
``` Splicing that over the block's span destroys three blocks. So any route to a parent `match` has to put the children back — and that is where the assumptions live. ## The question to answer Given a parent block whose corrected shallow form differs from its original shallow form, can the original children be re-inserted into the corrected parent at positions that are (a) determinable and (b) still correct after the correction? Concretely, `src/block-locator.js`'s `shallowMarkup()` removes each child's span and records nothing about where the seam was. The inverse operation needs those seams, and needs them to still be meaningful in text `canonicalize` may have re-indented, re-wrapped, or restructured around. ## Suggested method 1. Extend `shallowMarkup()` locally (spike only) to record each child's removal offset. 2. Correct the shallow parent, then re-insert children at the recorded seams, mapped through whatever the correction did to the surrounding text. 3. Verify the same way `wpbg-lsf` does: splice the reconstructed parent over the original span and re-validate the **whole document**, not the block alone — a parent's children must survive as blocks, which block-level validation would not catch. 4. Run it across the nested parents available: `title.html` L1 (3 children) and L6 (1 child), plus `deeply-nested-mismatched-closer.html`'s shape once made valid enough to reach Layer 2. ## What would make this a "no" Any of these is a sufficient reason to stop and record leaf-only as permanent: - The correction changes text *between* children, so the seams cannot be mapped without diffing — which reintroduces exactly the "was it corrected or just reformatted?" problem `wpbg-lsf` was designed to sidestep. - Re-inserting children yields a document that validates but whose child blocks have moved, changed nesting, or lost delimiter attributes. - The reconstruction only works when the parent's correction is confined to its opening tag — in which case say so plainly, since a narrower rule ("`match` for a parent only when the correction touches nothing but the wrapper element") may be worth more than a general one. ## Deliverable A verdict comment on this bead, and a findings file under `handoff/` if the reasoning is long enough to be worth keeping — matching how `wpbg-4n7` was settled in `handoff/2026-09-05-block-isolation-verdict-spike.md`. If the answer is yes, file the implementation as its own bead. If no, record why here and in `docs/adr/0002-search-is-byte-exact-or-absent.md`, so leaf-only reads as a decision rather than an omission.
